study_design_identified: Primary qualitative participatory study using focus group discussions (FGDs) and stakeholder participatory co-creation workshops
why_tool_chosen: The Methods section explicitly defines and reports the research as a primary qualitative study following COREQ guidelines (PDF p. 3), relying exclusively on focus group discussions and participatory stakeholder workshops analyzed via qualitative framework analysis in NVivo 12, with no quantitative survey, experimental, or quasi-experimental component; therefore, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the exact matching instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (1 Can't tell item on Q6 reflexivity; Yes on Q1-Q5 and Q7-Q9, with perceptual-only WASH outcomes)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly state the dual study objectives and corresponding research questions: (1) documenting how the co-creation process of informal social accountability mechanisms (iSAMs) operates in WASH service delivery in childcare centers, and (2) documenting how stakeholders self-evaluate the co-creation process in Nairobi's informal settlements.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Introduction (PDF p. 3); Methods - Study objectives (PDF p. 3)

domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative participatory methodology is well suited to exploring how childcare managers and parents collaboratively define informal accountability processes, negotiate shared norms, and subjectively appraise the benefits and barriers of co-creation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Introduction (PDF p. 3); Methods - Study design (PDF pp. 3-4)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors justify combining siloed formative FGDs (separate parent and manager groups) with joint multi-stakeholder participatory workshops and post-workshop reflection FGDs, grounded in Coleman's social capital framework, to enable bottom-up deliberation, consensus-building, and subsequent self-evaluation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Conceptual framework (PDF p. 3, Figure 1); Methods - Study design & Data collection process (PDF pp. 3-5, Figure 3)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors clearly explain purposive recruitment of 200 participants (34 childcare managers and 66 parents in each of Korogocho and Viwandani across 8 village units per site), selecting managers serving children across multiple units for diversity and parents with primary financial responsibility and longest tenure to support multi-session engagement. While purposive selection of long-staying, dedicated volunteers limits representativeness of transient families, the selection criteria are transparent and aligned with the participatory aims.
domain_ratings.where_found: Conceptual framework (PDF p. 3); Methods - Study setting & Target population, sampling and sample size (PDF pp. 4-5, Table 1, Figure 2)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: The setting and iterative data collection architecture (December 2021-May 2022) are well documented: 8 parent FGDs and 4 manager FGDs per site (8-10 participants, 45-60 mins) in community halls, followed by 4 participatory workshops (~50 participants, ~90 mins) and post-workshop self-evaluation FGDs (~45 mins), using trained moderators, note-takers, team leaders, audio recordings, flip charts, slides, and daily debriefings, although verbatim interview/workshop guides and data saturation are not explicitly detailed.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods - Data collection process & Data quality control (PDF p. 5, Figure 3)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the paper notes that APHRC has operated the NUHDSS in both settlements since 2002, that community-endorsed research assistants were recruited, and quotes participants praising researchers for listening to them, the authors do not critically examine their own positionality, institutional power dynamics, or how researcher facilitation of the co-creation workshops might have induced social desirability bias during the post-workshop self-evaluation FGDs.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods - Study setting & Data quality control (PDF pp. 4-5); Results - Positive self-evaluation (PDF pp. 9-10)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: Ethical approvals were obtained from AMREF Health Africa's ESRC (P747/2020), NACOSTI (NACOSTI/P/20/7726), LSTM, and APHRC internal review boards; written informed consent (including for photos/videos) was obtained from all participants, and transcripts used anonymized identifiers.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods - Data analysis & Ethical considerations (PDF p. 6); Ethics statement (PDF p. 13)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: Audio recordings were transcribed, translated from Swahili to English where necessary, and third-party cross-checked; framework analysis in NVivo 12 involved two researchers and five co-researchers independently reading transcripts to establish inter-coder agreement before consensus coding, charting, and mapping (Table 2). Findings are supported by diverse verbatim quotes across both settlements, sexes, and stakeholder roles, including contradictory/negative views.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods - Data analysis (PDF p. 6, Table 2); Results (PDF pp. 6-11)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly structured around the four co-created iSAM steps (defining accountability, action/information, judging/assessing performance, learning/adapting) toward meeting WASH needs (Figure 4) and balanced positive versus negative self-evaluation themes, explicitly linked back to the research questions.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results (PDF pp. 6-11, Table 2, Figure 4); Discussion (PDF pp. 11-12)

domain_ratings.justification: Narrative assessment: The study provides useful empirical insight into how parents and informal childcare center managers in low-income urban settlements conceptualize and negotiate informal accountability for under-5 WASH services where statutory provision is absent, identifying practical constraints (poverty, fee non-payment, time burdens, inconsistent commitment) alongside transferable participatory steps, though value for establishing effectiveness is constrained by the absence of objective WASH service or health measurements and reliance on two NUHDSS settlements.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable exploratory contribution to participatory urban WASH governance in informal childcare settings, tempered by perceptual-only WASH outcomes and local NUHDSS context
domain_ratings.where_found: Discussion, Strengths and limitations, & Conclusion (PDF pp. 11-12)

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Some concern: Formative FGDs enrolled 200 participants (100 per settlement), and four participatory workshops each convened ~50 prior FGD participants across December 2021-May 2022 (PDF p. 5), but exact longitudinal attendance, refusal, or drop-out rates across the multi-session series are not reported despite lack of consistent commitment emerging as a negative theme (Table 2, PDF p. 6).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable (qualitative design; high concern if interpreted causally): As an exploratory qualitative participatory study without a comparator arm or quantitative estimation, confounding factors (such as baseline center resources or longstanding APHRC NUHDSS presence) are not controlled.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak for formal law / Adequate for informal norms: Formal legal instruments (non-statutory status of under-5 childcare services, UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, SDG 6.b/17) appear only as background framing (PDF pp. 2, 11). Empirically, the study operationalizes informal social accountability mechanisms (iSAMs)—role expectations, fee/supply agreements, informal inspections, rewards, and exclusion sanctions—through stakeholder consensus rather than coding formal legal or municipal regulatory compliance.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate to high concern: Data were gathered via moderator-led FGDs and participatory workshops, with self-evaluation FGDs conducted immediately after each workshop by the same research team (PDF p. 5, Figure 3). Without critical reflexivity or independent evaluators, participant appraisals of the co-creation process are vulnerable to social desirability and acquiescence bias, and WASH improvements reflect perceived potential rather than observed facility changes.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak for physical WASH outcomes (perceptual/anticipated only): No structured facility audits, microbiological/water-supply measurements, or child health assessments were conducted; meeting children's WASH needs was documented solely through participants' qualitative perceptions and anticipated expectations of the co-created process (PDF pp. 6-10, 12).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Low to moderate concern: Reporting follows COREQ guidelines (PDF p. 3) and transparently presents both positive and negative stakeholder appraisals including resource, time, and commitment barriers (PDF pp. 6, 9-11), though the exact FGD and workshop topic guides are not provided in full and no pre-registered protocol is cited.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern: Purposive sampling across Korogocho and Viwandani NUHDSS sites selected childcare managers serving multiple village units and parents who were primary fee-payers with the longest center tenure, explicitly favoring dedicated volunteers likely to sustain multi-stage participation (PDF pp. 3, 5). More transient, newly enrolled, or financially marginalized parents and isolated centers are likely under-represented.

overall_narrative_summary: Chumo et al. (2023) report a primary qualitative participatory study (FGDs and multi-stakeholder workshops with 200 childcare managers and parents across Korogocho and Viwandani informal settlements in Nairobi) documenting the co-creation and stakeholder self-evaluation of informal social accountability mechanisms (iSAMs) for WASH delivery in childcare centers. Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, methodological reporting is strong across 8 of the 9 binary/ternary items (Q1-Q5, Q7-Q9 rated Yes): aims, participatory design, purposive sampling across village units, multi-stage data collection, multi-board ethical approvals, third-party transcript verification, NVivo framework analysis with inter-coder agreement, and balanced reporting of positive and negative appraisals are all clearly documented. The primary methodological weakness is Q6 (Can't tell): the authors do not critically examine researcher reflexivity, long-standing institutional presence (APHRC/NUHDSS), or facilitator-induced social desirability bias when participants evaluated workshops led by the research team. In addition, purposive selection of longest-tenured, dedicated parents limits representativeness, longitudinal workshop retention is not quantified, and WASH service improvements were captured solely as participant perceptions rather than verified facility or health outcomes.
where_found_summary: Study aims and COREQ/qualitative design in Abstract (PDF p. 1), Introduction (PDF p. 3), and Methods (PDF pp. 3-4); NUHDSS setting and purposive sampling of 200 managers/parents in Methods and Table 1 (PDF pp. 4-5); FGD/workshop procedures, quality control, NVivo 12 framework analysis, and ethics approvals in Methods and Figure 3 (PDF pp. 5-6, 13); thematic findings and verbatim quotes in Results, Table 2, and Figure 4 (PDF pp. 6-11); limitations and transferability in Discussion/Conclusion (PDF pp. 11-12).
